text: Cotonou. The night of the third of March, 1890.
A storm had battered the coast since seven in the evening, and the garrison of 359 men waited in the dark.
Most of them were African: Senegalese tirailleurs in red chéchias, and Gabonese who had landed from the cruiser Sané two weeks before. A few were European marine officers and artillerymen.
They had been warned by spies that an attack was coming, and they watched in thirds through the night.
Just before five, the lieutenant commanding the north bastion, a young marine officer named Compérat, heard something moving in the brush. He warned his men in a whisper.
Then bells sounded. Ten paces from the wall, an army rose.
At its head marched the women soldiers of the Kingdom of Dahomey. So what can we actually prove about them?
This is the story of the women soldiers of Dahomey.
Their name was Agojie. It means, roughly, make way for me, or I fall on you. They were a standing corps, probably formed as a palace guard in the 1720s.
By the late 1870s, they numbered about 1,500.
Their training was brutal: climbing thorn hedges, wrestling, survival exercises lasting days.
They fought with muskets, blades and amulets. Their colonel wore silver horns in her hair.
And according to Governor Bayol, who saw the march, the women led the column. Behind them came the fetish priests and the royal guards. And behind them, the regular troops.
The attack came in two columns.
The left, with the women's regiment and perhaps a thousand men, struck the half-built fort on the lagoon.
The right was delayed by the thick woods and came later. Nothing came at the centre.
Several thousand attackers in total. The sources disagree, and no reliable count exists.

One eyewitness disagrees. Foà, the trader who was there, writes that the corps of women soldiers was not engaged that day, and that a few took part of their own accord, while the rest watched from a short distance.
Two accounts put the women at the head of the column. One says they watched it.
cut_after: We have gone with the two, and told you about the one.

text: The women and men pulled apart the stakes of the palisade and fired through the gaps. Some climbed onto the stockade and were bayoneted, and their bodies fell inside.
Compérat was hit three times. One bullet broke his shoulder blade. He stayed in command and told his sergeant: Stay at your post. I am wounded too, and I am not complaining.
On the left, the Agor post was briefly abandoned. Lemoyne's second company of Senegalese tirailleurs arrived, fired at ten paces, and charged with the bayonet.
Some attackers lay flat to let the charge pass over them, then rose and fired into the tirailleurs' backs. One section turned about and killed them.
The cruiser Sané shelled the woods from offshore.

At first light, a section of the fourth company reached the fort with bayonets fixed, and the fighting became hand-to-hand. By dawn, Oudard's section opened oblique fire from the centre, and Pansier's company completed the rout on the right.

At 6:15, the Dahomeans attacked again and were stopped at two hundred metres. They re-formed several times, and each time the shells from the Sané and the three-gun battery broke them up. At nine, the last attackers left. The fight had lasted about four and a half hours.

Eight French soldiers were killed, including two artillerymen hit at their guns. Twenty-six were wounded. Inside the lines, 127 of the dead were counted. Seven of them were women. Another count exists that gives a different number, but the figure from the primary account is 127.
According to Governor Bayol, a young woman soldier he had watched carry out her first execution in Abomey was at Cotonou. He had called her Nanisca.
He saw his chief gunner beheaded by a fighter he recognised as her, and later found her body, with a curved cleaver tied to her wrist and a carbine covered in cowries.
Another French account says a woman soldier killed the gunner, but does not name her. The identification is Bayol's alone.
The dead were beheaded, and their heads were sent in sealed sacks to the French-allied king of Porto-Novo.
Foà, a trader who was present, records that two or three women were found alive on the field. One was very young and gravely wounded. None survived.
Who were these women, and what had prepared them for this?
A standing army of women, probably formed as a palace guard in the 1720s. About 600 from the 1760s to the 1840s. King Gezo expanded the corps to as many as 6,000. By the late 1870s, perhaps 1,500.

Their training included climbing thorn hedges, wrestling, and survival exercises of up to nine days. They were not a legend invented by a newspaper or a film. They were a real institution, with a structure, a chain of command, and a history longer than most European armies.
But the images we often see are not the battle.
An illustration from 1851 by Frederick Forbes shows a woman soldier named Seh-Dong-Hong-Beh. In the full plate, she is holding a severed head. It is not a photograph, and it is not 1890.
A postcard from the early 1900s by François-Edmond Fortier is captioned as showing survivors. It is not the battle either.

French newspapers printed dramatic images within days of the fighting. One showed women holding severed heads, but Le Petit Parisien gave them horned helmets that a historian has called certainly fictitious.
And some of the photographs circulating online show performers at European exhibitions, not soldiers at war.

Objects taken from the battlefield on the fourth of March are in the Musée du quai Branly in Paris today. Nine items, including necklaces, amulets, a whistle and a horn, were gifted by a trader named Foà in 1891.
Some contain human remains and are subject to restitution claims by Benin.
cut_before: The museum notes say some were taken from a dead woman soldier.

text: The war did not end at Cotonou. In October 1890, a deal was reached at Ouidah. Dahomey respected the Porto-Novo protectorate and accepted the French occupation of Cotonou for an annual payment. But the French parliament never ratified it.

In 1892, France returned with a larger force under General Dodds and the Foreign Legion, and a new rifle appeared. The famous dawn attack at Dogba, with soldiers running from tents, belongs to that war, not to this one.
The women soldiers fought again. And a French report from April 1890 already called them harpies drunk on trade gin. That is a colonial voice, not a fact.
The Kingdom of Dahomey resisted French expansion. It also practised slavery. Both are true.
The last known veteran, Nawi, died in 1979. She had been a soldier in a kingdom that no longer existed, fighting a war she did not start.

The images we have are not the battle. The battle is in the words of the people who were there. An officer who stayed at his post with a broken shoulder. Governor Bayol, who watched a young woman he called Nanisca. A trader who picked up objects from the dead and sent them to a museum.
The women soldiers of Dahomey were real. Getting the date and the evidence right is how we tell their story without inventing it.
